title: Key Canonicalizer, Collision Diagnostics, and TTL Shepherd for Safe KV Apply
creator: Aisha Raman
description: Build a production-ready key canonicalization component (Key Canonicalizer) plus a set of collision-detection diagnostics and a TTL Shepherd that together enable automated, safe application of prefix/KV cache policies. The feature reduces cache fragmentation, prevents hot key collisions, and allows incremental TTL annealing with automatic rollback triggers. This ticket covers design, prototype, integration tests, dashboards, and a staged rollout plan.
background: Recent incidents showed cost regressions when new prefix rules unintentionally produced high cardinality key variants (different trailing context tokens and user identifiers). Batching behavior amplified cost because small changes to key shapes caused lower hit rates and larger per-token billing. Existing work focuses on TTL heuristics, but we lack a deterministic canonicalizer and collision observability. This increases risk when autotuning TTL/prefix policies across Dedicated and Hosted fleets.
goals: Implement deterministic key canonicalization policies with pluggable normalization rules (affix stripping, case normalization, length bucketing, and optional fingerprinting).
Create a lightweight collision-detection pipeline that samples requests and emits a collision score and cardinality delta per prefix.
Design a TTL Shepherd: staged annealing schedule, canary rollout orchestration, and automated rollback on defined safety signals.
Integrate with batching heuristics so canonicalization is batching-aware (avoid canonicalization that reduces batchability).
Provide dashboards, alerts, and a playbook for operators and SREs.
acceptance_criteria: Canonicalizer validated in unit tests with >98% determinism across inputs and clear opt-out hooks.
Collision detector produces per-prefix cardinality and collision_score metric; validated on historical traces with synthetic collisions injected.
TTL Shepherd supports 4-stage rollout (shadow -> canary 1% -> canary 10% -> full 100%) with automatic rollback when any safety rule trips.

End-to-end integration test demonstrating no more than 1.5% drop in system-wide hit-rate during a staged apply on representative workload, and cost delta < 3% after anneal stabilization for the test cluster.
Grafana dashboard and alert runbook linked and reviewed by SRE and PM.
design_decisions: Use deterministic canonicalization rather than ML-based clustering to keep behavior debuggable and reversible.
Prefer lossless canonicalization where possible; where lossy (fingerprinting) is used we add an explicit TTL guard and require security_review_required flag.
Collision detection will run as a sampled sidecar pipeline for 48 hours during shadow to avoid perf impact on hot paths.
Batching-aware rule: avoid canonicalization that increases variance of token sequence lengths within the same prefix bucket by more than 20%.
rollout_plan: 1) Deploy canonicalizer+collision-sidecar to runtime in shadow mode (0% traffic): collect 48h metrics. 2) Run automated analyzer to compute collision_score, batchability_impact, and simulated hit-rate effect. 3) If metrics pass threshold, start staged TTL Shepherd: shadow -> 1% canary (24h) -> 10% canary (24h) -> 100% ramp. 4) At each stage evaluate safety gates and commit or rollback. 5) If rollback: revert canonicalizer via feature flag and set TTL Shepherd to previous stable TTL schedule.
safety_gates: token_cost_increase > 5% over baseline for the test window
implementation_notes: Canonicalizer is implemented as a small deterministic transform layer in front of the KV encoder. Rules are expressed as an ordered pipeline: token-affix-stripper -> normalization -> length-bucket -> optional fingerprint. Each rule has metadata (stable_id, reversible flag). We expose a 'trace-id' header to map canonicalized keys back to original examples during debugging. Collision sidecar samples 0.1% of traffic by default, collecting (original_key, canonical_key, prefix) and computing approximate cardinality using HyperLogLog offline. The TTL Shepherd accepts a JSON policy describing anneal steps and includes a safety-check API used by the rollout controller.
tradeoffs: Deterministic rules are easier to audit but may miss some semantic equivalences that an ML model could find.
Sampling for collision detection reduces runtime overhead but delays detection of rare collisions; we compensate via targeted full-scan jobs on suspect prefixes.
Fingerprinting reduces cardinality but is lossy; we gate it behind strict thresholds and require review for security-sensitive prefixes.
